moment: My friend can tickle me easily, but when I try to tickle myself, nothing happens.
question: Why can’t I tickle myself?
summary: Your brain predicts what your own movements will feel like and turns those sensations down. A tickle only works when it’s a surprise.

beats.title: You decide to move
beats.text: You reach for your own ribs. Your motor cortex sends commands to your arm and fingers.

beats.title: A copy of the plan
beats.text: A copy of that movement command goes to the cerebellum, like your brain sending itself a note: here’s what I’m about to do.

beats.title: Prediction
beats.text: The cerebellum predicts exactly what the touch will feel like: where, when and how hard.

beats.title: Touch arrives, turned down
beats.text: The real touch signal reaches your body map. Because it matches the prediction, the response here is dialled down. No surprise, no tickle.

beats.title: When a friend does it
beats.text: When someone else tickles you, there’s no prediction to cancel it out. The touch is unexpected, your body map responds fully, and you squirm and laugh.

whyItFelt: Your brain is constantly predicting the results of your own actions so it can focus on what’s unexpected. That’s useful: it’s how you can tell a spider on your arm from your own sleeve brushing it. Self-tickling fails because it’s too predictable.

tryThis.title: Feel the difference
tryThis.text: Lightly stroke your palm with your own finger, then have someone else do the same. The second usually feels stronger, because your brain couldn’t predict it.

tryThis.title: Add a delay
tryThis.text: In one experiment, people tickled themselves through a robot. Adding a delay of about a fifth of a second made the touch feel more ticklish, because it no longer matched the prediction.

finePrint: The robot studies used small groups of people, but many later studies support the idea that the brain dampens sensations it caused itself.

sources.title: Central cancellation of self-produced tickle sensation
